'''Wilfrid Joseph Dixon''' (December 13, 1915&nbsp;– September 20, 2008) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[statistician]]. He made notable contributions to [[nonparametric statistics]], [[statistical education]] and [[experimental design]].

A native of [[Portland, Oregon]], Dixon received a bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[Oregon State University|Oregon State College]] in 1938. He continued his graduate studies at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]], where he earned a master's degree in 1939. Under supervision of [[Samuel S. Wilks]], he then earned a Ph.D. in mathematical statistics from Princeton in 1944.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wilfrid J. Dixon *44 |work=[[Princeton Alumni Weekly]] |date=September 23, 2009 |url=https://paw.princeton.edu/memorial/wilfrid-j-dixon-44 }}</ref> During [[World War II]], he was an operations analyst on [[Guam]].

Dixon was on the faculties at [[University of Oklahoma|Oklahoma]] (1942–1943), [[University of Oregon|Oregon]] (1946–1955), and [[University of California, Los Angeles|UCLA]] (1955–1986, then emeritus). While at Oregon, Dixon (together with [[Alexander M. Mood]]) described and provided theory and estimation methods for the adaptive [[Up-and-Down_Designs|Up-and-Down experimental design]], which was new and poorly documented at the time.<ref name=DixMood48>{{cite journal |last1=Dixon|first1=WJ |last2=Mood | first2=AM |author-link2=Alexander M. Mood |title=A method for obtaining and analyzing sensitivity data |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |year=1948 |volume=43 |issue=241 |pages=109–126 |doi=10.1080/01621459.1948.10483254}}</ref> This article became the cornerstone publication for up-and-down, a family of designs used in many scientific, engineering and medical fields, and to which Dixon continued to contribute in later years. In 1951 Dixon, together with [[Frank J. Massey|Frank Massey]], published a statistics textbook - the first such textbook intended to a non-mathematical audience.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dixon |first1=WJ |last2=Massey |first2=FJ |author-link2=Frank J. Massey|title=Introduction to statistical analysis |date=1951 |publisher=McGraw-Hill}}</ref> In 1955 he was elected as a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]].<ref>[http://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm View/Search Fellows of the ASA] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160616161612/https://www.amstat.org/awards/fellowslist.cfm |date=2016-06-16 }}, accessed 2016-07-23.</ref>

In the 1960s at UCLA, Dixon developed [[BMDP]], a statistical software package for biomedical analyses.<ref>{{cite web |title=Oral History of Wilfrid J. (Wil) Dixon and Linda Glassner: Interviewed by Luanne Johnson |date=March 27, 1986 |url=http://archive.computerhistory.org/resources/access/text/2012/04/102658169-05-01-acc.pdf }}</ref>

His daughter, [[Janet D. Elashoff]], is also a statistician who became a UCLA faculty member, and was named an ASA fellow in 1978.<ref>{{citation|url=https://cwstat.org/about/people/asa-fellows/|title=ASA Fellows|date=29 March 2016|publisher=[[Caucus for Women in Statistics]]|accessdate=2017-10-24|archive-date=2017-10-25|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171025075400/https://cwstat.org/about/people/asa-fellows/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In December 2008 she funded the American Statistical Association's [https://www.amstat.org/your-career/awards/w-j-dixon-award-for-excellence-in-statistical-consulting W. J. Dixon Award for Excellence in Statistical Consulting] in his honor.<ref>{{citation|url=http://amstat.org/ASA/Your-Career/Awards/W-J-Dixon-Award-for-Excellence-in-Statistical-Consulting.aspx|title=W. J. Dixon Award for Excellence in Statistical Consulting|publisher=American Statistical Association|accessdate=2017-10-24}}</ref>
